content: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice have the potential to interact with a wide range of medications. This is primarily due to the high concentrations of compounds such as naringin, bergamottin, and dihydroxybergamottin found in grapefruit. These compounds interfere with the activity of the intestinal enzyme cytochrome P450 isoform CYP3A4. Additionally, bioactive compounds in grapefruit juice may also affect p-glycoprotein and organic anion transporting polypeptides (OATPs), which can either increase or decrease the bioavailability of certain drugs. Benzodiazepines, including alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium), midazolam (Versed), lorazepam (Ativan), oxazepam, and chlordiazepoxide (Librium), are among the drugs affected by grapefruit juice. The antihistamines astemizole and fexofenadine are also influenced by grapefruit juice. Other drugs impacted by grapefruit juice include statins such as atorvastatin, lovastatin, and simvastatin. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, including felodipine (Plendil), nicardipine (Cardene), difedipine, nisoldipine (Sular), and nitrendipine (Bayotensin), are also affected. Losartan (Cozaar), repaglinide (Prandin), and verapamil (Calan SR, Covera HS, Isoptin SR, Verelan) are additional examples. Antiarrhythmic drugs such as amiodarone (Cordarone), quinidine (Quinidex, Cardioquin, Quinora), disopyramide (Norpace), propafenone (Rythmol), and carvedilol are also influenced by grapefruit juice. Medications for male impotence, including sildenafil (Viagra), tadalafil (Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra), are affected as well. Anti-migraine drugs such as ergotamine (Cafergot, Ergomar) and nimodipine (Nimotop) are also on the list of drugs that interact with grapefruit juice. Grapefruit juice interacts with many oral medications by inhibiting the activity of certain intestinal enzymes, particularly CYP3A4 and CYP1A2, which are part of the cytochrome P450 enzyme family. These enzymes are responsible for metabolizing many drugs. When inhibited by grapefruit juice, the serum concentrations of these drugs can increase, potentially leading to toxic levels. This is especially dangerous for drugs with a low therapeutic index, where even a small increase in blood concentration can result in toxicity. It is important to note that grapefruit juice only inhibits these enzymes in the intestines and does not affect their activity in the liver or other parts of the body. Additionally, it does not impact drugs administered via injection. The extent of the interaction varies significantly between individuals and even between different samples of grapefruit juice, making it difficult to predict the effect in advance. Recent research suggests that furanocoumarins, rather than flavonoids, may be the primary compounds responsible for these drug interactions. Among the flavonoids, naringin is present in the highest concentration in grapefruit juice and is metabolized in humans to naringenin. Other flavonoids are present in lower concentrations. Orange juice, in contrast, contains lower levels of naringin and instead contains hesperetin, which is sometimes recommended as a substitute. Lime juice and Seville orange juice can also inhibit drug metabolism, as can apple juice with certain medications.
